title: Debt is sized by its tightest test
summary: A lender does not decide how much to lend from one ratio; it runs several tests and lends the smallest answer. This lesson teaches debt service coverage, debt yield, loan-to-value and loan-to-cost, how to find the binding limit, and why the choice between fixed and floating rates decides whether the loan survives a bad year.
body:
A loan is sized by whichever of the lender's tests gives the smallest number, and that test is called the binding limit. Know the binding limit before the meeting, and know what happens to coverage if the interest rate moves, and you will never be surprised by a term sheet.

Recall

Q. Who may sign a loan agreement on behalf of a project company?

A. Only a person the company has authorised, usually by a directors' resolution recorded in the minute book that names the signatory and approves the borrowing. A lender's counsel will ask to see that resolution before funding.

Q. What is residual land value?

A. The most a developer can pay for land and still earn a required profit: the finished value, minus every cost, minus the profit, leaves what the land is worth to that project.

Q. Why is absorption expressed as a number rather than a feeling?

A. Because a lender and an investor need units or square feet taken up per month to build a timeline. "Strong demand" cannot be put into a cash flow; "eight units a month in a market that took ten last year" can.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, debt is the cheapest money in most projects and the most dangerous. It is cheap because it is repaid first. It is dangerous because it must be paid on a fixed timetable whether or not the building is doing well. A developer who understands how a lender sizes a loan can predict the offer, design the project so the offer is enough, and refuse a loan that looks generous but breaks in an ordinary downturn. A developer who does not understands debt only as a headline amount and a headline rate, which are the two least informative numbers on the page.

Four tests, in plain English

Every lender asks four questions, in some form. Can the income pay the loan? Does the loan make sense if the lender has to take the property back? Is the loan small compared with what the property is worth? Is the loan small compared with what it cost to build?

The first question is answered by the debt service coverage ratio (DSCR): net operating income (NOI), the income left after operating expenses and before loan payments, divided by annual debt service, meaning interest and any principal repayment for the year. A coverage of 1.25 means the income covers the payments one and a quarter times. The second is answered by debt yield: NOI divided by the loan amount, expressed as a percentage. It tells the lender what income it would earn on its money if it owned the building, and it ignores the interest rate entirely. The third is loan-to-value (LTV): the loan divided by appraised value. The fourth is loan-to-cost (LTC): the loan divided by total project cost, the test construction lenders lean on because, before completion, value is a forecast and cost is a fact.

The minimum coverage, minimum debt yield and maximum percentages are commercial practice set by each lender's credit policy, not standards or law, and they move with the market. The numbers below are hypothetical.

Finding the binding limit

Here is the first worked example. A hypothetical stabilised apartment building has NOI of 1,000,000 dollars a year, an appraised value of 15,000,000 dollars, and cost 13,000,000 dollars to build. The lender's term sheet asks for coverage of at least 1.25, a debt yield of at least 11 percent, loan-to-value no higher than 65 percent and loan-to-cost no higher than 75 percent. For coverage, assume a hypothetical loan constant of 8 percent, meaning that each year interest and principal together come to 8 percent of the original loan.

Run each test. Coverage: the most the building can pay is 1,000,000 divided by 1.25, which is 800,000 a year, and 800,000 divided by 0.08 is a loan of 10,000,000. Debt yield: 1,000,000 divided by 0.11 is a loan of about 9,090,000. Loan-to-value: 65 percent of 15,000,000 is 9,750,000. Loan-to-cost: 75 percent of 13,000,000 is 9,750,000. The smallest answer is the debt yield, at about 9,090,000 dollars. That is the binding limit, and the loan offered will be close to it however strong the other three tests look.

The professional habit is to lay the four answers side by side in one table on page one, with the binding test highlighted. That table tells you where to spend effort. If debt yield binds, a lower interest rate will not raise the loan by a dollar; only more NOI will. If coverage binds, a lower rate or a longer amortisation will help. If loan-to-value binds, the appraisal is the lever.

Say that out loud now.

Fixed, floating and the hedge

A fixed-rate loan charges the same rate for its term. A floating-rate loan charges a margin over a published benchmark rate, so the payment rises and falls with that benchmark. Floating is often cheaper on the day you sign and more expensive on the day it hurts.

The second worked example shows why. Take a hypothetical 9,000,000 dollar loan, interest only, on the same building. At an all-in floating rate of 6 percent, interest is 540,000 dollars and coverage is 1,000,000 divided by 540,000, about 1.85. If the rate rises to 8 percent, interest is 720,000 and coverage falls to about 1.39. At 9 percent, interest is 810,000 and coverage is about 1.23, below a 1.25 covenant, and the building has not lost a single tenant.

A hedge is a contract that limits that exposure. An interest rate cap pays the borrower whenever the benchmark rises above a chosen strike, so the effective rate cannot climb past it; it is bought for an upfront premium. An interest rate swap exchanges the floating payment for a fixed one, turning a floating loan into a fixed loan in effect, but it can cost money to unwind early. If our 9,000,000 loan carried a cap that held the all-in rate at 7.5 percent, the worst-case interest would be 675,000 and coverage would stay at about 1.48. The cap is the price of knowing your worst year in advance.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is sizing a floating-rate loan to today's rate and assuming the rate will stay put long enough to refinance. The control is to calculate coverage at the rate cap strike, or at a stressed rate if there is no cap, and to require that the project still meets its covenant there. If it does not, borrow less, buy the cap, or fix the rate.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner shops for the largest loan and the lowest rate, and treats the term sheet's coverage and debt yield numbers as paperwork. Those numbers are the loan. They decide the amount, and they decide when the lender can stop you taking cash out of your own building.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: interest is often deductible and hedge payments may be treated differently from interest, so the after-tax cost of fixed and floating can differ; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: many loans add personal guarantees or recourse carve-outs, so the binding limit is not the only number that reaches you. Banking: the coverage covenant becomes a running test, and breaching it can trap cash or trigger default. Governance: the borrowing and any hedge each need a properly authorised resolution. Estate: a guarantee can survive you and bind your estate, so record every one where your executor will find it. Exit: fixed-rate loans and swaps can carry prepayment or breakage costs that decide whether an early sale or refinance is worth doing.

Callback

In week 10 we learned that value is NOI divided by a capitalisation rate. Every lender test in this lesson starts from the same NOI. That is why a weak NOI hurts you twice: it lowers value, which shrinks the loan-to-value answer, and it lowers coverage and debt yield directly. Protect NOI and you protect every test at once.

Recap

A lender runs coverage, debt yield, loan-to-value and loan-to-cost, and lends the smallest answer. Find the binding test and you know which lever to pull. Floating rates move coverage without any change in the building, so test coverage at the cap or a stressed rate, and hedge or borrow less if the covenant fails there.

Next: Ford, with Roman, takes apart a composite collapse: the floating-rate loan, the coverage breach and the guarantee that was called.
checklist: Run all four tests: coverage, debt yield, loan-to-value and loan-to-cost
Put the four loan amounts side by side and mark the binding limit
State the loan constant or rate used for the coverage test
Recalculate coverage at the cap strike or a stressed rate
Confirm the covenant still holds at that rate
Price a cap and a swap before choosing floating debt
Record every guarantee and recourse carve-out attached to the loan
Run the Six-Lens Check before signing the term sheet

speak: Mr Shabazz, here is debt sizing in one minute. A lender runs four tests and lends the smallest answer. Debt service coverage is net operating income divided by annual debt service. Debt yield is net operating income divided by the loan, and it ignores the interest rate. Loan-to-value divides the loan by appraised value, and loan-to-cost divides it by what the project cost. On a building earning 1,000,000 a year, worth 15,000,000 and costing 13,000,000, the tests gave 10,000,000, 9,090,000, 9,750,000 and 9,750,000, so debt yield binds and a cheaper rate will not raise the loan. Floating rates move coverage with no change in the building: a 9,000,000 loan covers 1.85 times at 6 percent and only 1.23 at 9. terms: Debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) — net operating income divided by annual interest and principal payments on the loan.
Debt yield — net operating income divided by the loan amount, a test of the loan's size that ignores the interest rate.
Loan-to-cost (LTC) — the loan divided by total project cost, the main sizing test before a building is complete.

hostile.q: Your coverage is 1.85. Why should I care that you are on a floating rate?
hostile.a: Because 1.85 is at today's rate. At 9 percent all-in, the same building covers about 1.23 and breaches a 1.25 covenant with no change in occupancy. So I will buy a cap that holds the all-in rate at 7.5 percent, which keeps coverage near 1.48 in the worst case, and the cap will be pledged to you for the term of the loan.

title: The floating loan, the coverage breach and the called guarantee
summary: A composite case: a sound apartment building, a floating-rate loan sized at a low rate, a cap that expired too early, and a guarantee that sprang on a coverage test. Ford, with Roman, takes it through seven steps and finds the root cause in how the debt was sized, not in how the building performed.
rule: Rule 36: I never sign floating-rate debt unless the project still meets its coverage covenant at the hedged or stressed rate for the full term, and I never sign a guarantee whose trigger is a test I have not stressed at that rate.
body:
This building did not fail. Its debt did. The tenants kept paying, the occupancy held, and the owner still lost the property and part of his personal net worth, because the loan was sized to one interest rate and lived through another.

Recall

Q. What is the binding limit in loan sizing?

A. The smallest loan produced by the lender's tests: coverage, debt yield, loan-to-value and loan-to-cost. That test decides the amount.

Q. In the week 34 checkpoint, why did we refuse to let a site's value depend on infrastructure someone else controls?

A. Because the project and its financing must survive that dependency arriving late. The same logic applies to anything outside your control, including interest rates.

Q. What does competing supply do to a feasibility study?

A. It reduces the share of demand your project can capture, slows absorption, and pushes revenue later, so it must be counted unit by unit, not mentioned in passing.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is a composite example, built from patterns that recur in rising-rate periods; the names and numbers are hypothetical. It matters because it shows the commonest way a careful developer loses a good asset: not through bad construction or bad tenants, but through a debt structure that only works in one rate environment. Roman assists today because the failure sits where risk and the lender's view meet.

Step 1: the timeline

Year 0: a developer completes and leases a hypothetical 120-unit apartment building. NOI settles at 1,500,000 dollars a year. He refinances the construction loan with a five-year floating-rate loan of 18,000,000 dollars, interest only. At the all-in rate of the day, 5 percent, interest is 900,000 and coverage is about 1.67. He buys a two-year interest rate cap because the lender requires one, and the two-year cap is the cheapest that satisfies the term sheet. Year 2: the cap expires. The lender's documents require a replacement cap, but replacement caps now cost several times more, because rates have risen. Year 3: the all-in rate reaches 8.5 percent. Interest is 1,530,000 dollars. Coverage is about 0.98: the building no longer covers its own interest. Year 3, second quarter: the coverage covenant of 1.20 is breached, a cash sweep traps every spare dollar, reserves run out, and a springing guarantee converts into full recourse against the developer. Year 4: the lender enforces.

Step 2: the key decisions

Three decisions mattered. Sizing the loan to the day's rate. Buying the shortest cap the lender would accept. Signing a guarantee that sprang on a coverage breach rather than only on fraud or misconduct.

Step 3: the assumptions

The developer assumed rates would stay near where they were for long enough to refinance into fixed-rate debt. He assumed a replacement cap would cost about what the first one did. He assumed the guarantee was a formality because the building was performing. Each assumption was about something outside his control, written down as though it were a fact.

Say that out loud now.

Step 4: the incentives

The lender was paid a margin over the benchmark and was protected by the cap and the guarantee, so a larger loan suited it. The broker was paid on the size of the loan placed. The cap seller was paid on the cap sold, and a shorter cap was an easier sale. The developer was rewarded with cash out at closing, because a larger loan returned more of his equity. Nobody in the room was paid to ask what happened in year three.

Step 5: the warning signs ignored

The lender's own term sheet required the cap to be replaced on expiry, which told anyone reading it that expiry was a real event. The forward rate curve, the market's own published expectation of future rates, was already rising at closing. And the coverage at the cap strike had never been calculated: had it been, it would have shown the loan only worked while the cap was alive.

Step 6: the point of no return

The point of no return was the cap's expiry in year 2. Until then, the developer could have sold, paid down the loan with new equity, or bought a longer cap at a price that was painful but survivable. Once rates rose and the cap lapsed, every option cost more than the equity left in the deal. The guarantee made it personal.

Step 7: the root cause

The root cause was sizing a five-year floating loan to a single rate observed at closing, and hedging only two of the five years. The building's performance was never the problem. Here is the arithmetic that should have been run at closing. Five-year cover at a stressed all-in rate of, say, 8 percent: interest of 1,440,000 against NOI of 1,500,000, coverage of about 1.04, below the 1.20 covenant. To meet 1.20 at 8 percent, interest could be no more than 1,250,000, which supports a loan of about 15,600,000. The developer borrowed about 2,400,000 dollars more than the building could carry in a stressed year.

A second worked example shows the guarantee's cost. Suppose the guarantee was capped at 25 percent of the loan. That is 4,500,000 dollars of personal exposure, triggered not by any misconduct but by a ratio the developer had not stressed. Roman's lender view: a springing guarantee on a financial covenant is effectively a promise that the borrower will fund losses in exactly the year he is least able to.

What a careful version would have looked like

Run the same building again with the discipline Roman would insist on. The developer sizes the loan at a stressed all-in rate of 8 percent and a 1.20 covenant, which gives about 15,600,000. He buys a cap for the full five years, or, if a five-year cap costs too much, he buys a three-year cap and funds a reserve at closing equal to a dealer's quote for the remaining two years. He negotiates the guarantee down to fraud, misconduct and environmental losses, offering a debt service reserve of, say, six months of interest in its place. He takes about 2,400,000 dollars less cash out at closing. That is the visible cost. The invisible benefit is that in year three, with rates at 8.5 percent, interest on 15,600,000 is 1,326,000 and coverage is about 1.13: below the covenant, but the reserve buys time, the capped rate holds the actual payment lower, and no guarantee has sprung. He can sell or recapitalise on his own timetable rather than the lender's.

The lesson is not that floating debt is wrong. It is that floating debt is a bet on a path of rates, and the bet must be sized so that losing it costs you the upside, not the asset.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a hedge that ends before the loan does. The control is to require that the hedge term matches the loan term, or that the replacement cost is reserved in cash at closing, and to size the loan so the covenant holds at the strike.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads "guarantee: springing" and assumes springing means unlikely. It means automatic once the trigger is hit. Read the trigger, then stress it.

The prevention rule

Rule 36: I never sign floating-rate debt unless the project still meets its coverage covenant at the hedged or stressed rate for the full term, and I never sign a guarantee whose trigger is a test I have not stressed at that rate.

Callback

In week 2 we learned the pre-mortem: imagine the project has failed and write down why. Run that exercise on any floating-rate loan and the first sentence almost writes itself: rates rose after the hedge expired. A pre-mortem that produces that sentence in five minutes is worth more than a term sheet that hides it for five years.

Recap

A performing building was lost because its debt was sized to one rate, hedged for two years of five, and backed by a guarantee that sprang on coverage. The root cause was the sizing, not the asset. Size to the stressed rate, hedge to the term, and read every guarantee trigger.

Next: Roman, on the money: how leverage, rates and hedges move cash yield, IRR and your own balance sheet.
checklist: Calculate coverage at the cap strike and at a stressed rate
Confirm the hedge term matches the loan term
Price the replacement cap before closing, not at expiry
Reserve the replacement cost if the hedge is shorter than the loan
Read every guarantee trigger and note any financial covenant
Run a five-minute pre-mortem on every floating-rate loan
Size the loan so the covenant holds at the stressed rate
State Rule 36 before signing

speak: Mr Shabazz, this composite case in one minute. A developer refinanced a well-leased apartment building with an 18,000,000 dollar floating loan, interest only, at 5 percent, for coverage of about 1.67. He bought a two-year cap on a five-year loan. When the cap expired, rates had risen and the replacement cost several times more. At 8.5 percent the building covered only 0.98 times, the 1.20 covenant was breached, cash was swept, and a springing guarantee became full recourse. The building never lost a tenant. The root cause was sizing to one rate and hedging two years of five. At a stressed 8 percent, the building could carry about 15,600,000, not 18,000,000. terms: Interest rate cap — a contract, bought for an upfront premium, that pays the borrower when a benchmark rate rises above a set strike, limiting the effective rate.
Springing guarantee — a guarantee that becomes enforceable automatically when a stated trigger occurs.
Forward rate curve — the market's published expectation of future benchmark rates, derived from current prices.

hostile.q: Your cap runs for two years and the loan runs for five. What happens in year three?
hostile.a: Nothing I have not already paid for. I have sized the loan so coverage holds at 1.20 at a stressed 8 percent, and I am funding a reserve at closing equal to the quoted cost of a replacement cap. If the market moves further, the reserve and the lower leverage carry the loan; I am not relying on rates staying put.

title: When borrowing raises your return, and when it quietly lowers it
summary: Debt raises the return on equity only while the asset earns more than the debt costs. This lesson shows positive and negative leverage with worked numbers, prices the trade between fixed, floating and capped debt, and closes with Warrick's Wealth Ledger on guarantees and liquidity.
body:
Leverage is a magnifier with a switch. When the property yields more than the loan costs, debt raises the return on your equity; when the loan costs more than the property yields, the same debt drags it down, and nothing about the building has to change for the switch to flip.

Recall

Q. In the composite case, what was the root cause?

A. Sizing a five-year floating loan to one rate observed at closing and hedging only two years. The building performed; the debt did not.

Q. What is the residual approach to land value?

A. Start from the finished value, subtract every cost and the required profit, and what remains is the most the project can pay for land.

Q. What does a go or no-go gate in feasibility require?

A. A stated threshold, decided before the numbers are run, that the project must clear to proceed, so the decision is not made by enthusiasm after the fact.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, most developers believe debt always improves returns because it usually did in the deals they remember. It improves returns only under one condition. If you know that condition, you can decide how much to borrow by arithmetic rather than by habit, and you can see the year in which your own loan starts working against you.

Positive and negative leverage

Plain English first. The property earns a yield: NOI divided by what it cost. The loan has a cost: the interest rate, or more precisely the loan constant if principal is being repaid. If the property's yield is above the loan's cost, each borrowed dollar earns more than it costs and the surplus goes to equity. That is positive leverage. If the yield is below the cost, each borrowed dollar loses money and equity pays the difference. That is negative leverage.

The first worked example. A hypothetical project cost 10,000,000 dollars and earns NOI of 700,000, a 7 percent yield on cost. The developer borrows 6,000,000 interest only and puts in 4,000,000 of equity. At a 5 percent rate, interest is 300,000 and cash flow to equity is 400,000, a cash-on-cash return of 10 percent on the 4,000,000. Without the loan, equity would have earned 7 percent. Debt added three points.

Now move the rate to 8 percent. Interest is 480,000, cash flow to equity is 220,000, and cash-on-cash falls to 5.5 percent. The unlevered building still earns 7 percent. The loan has turned a 7 percent asset into a 5.5 percent investment for its owner. The switch sits at exactly the point where the rate equals the yield on cost.

Say that out loud now.

Leverage and IRR

The internal rate of return (IRR), the single annual rate that makes the present value of every cash flow equal zero, behaves the same way but more violently, because it includes the sale. If value grows, the gain on sale lands entirely on a smaller equity cheque, so levered IRR can rise far above unlevered IRR. If value falls, the loss lands on that same small cheque first, because the lender is repaid before equity. A modest fall in value can take levered IRR negative while the unlevered IRR is still positive. So the right question is never "does debt raise my IRR?" but "in which cases, and by how much does it deepen the loss in the others?"

What a hedge costs, and what it buys

The second worked example compares three ways to borrow the same 6,000,000 for three years. These are hypothetical prices, and real pricing moves daily. Option one: a fixed rate of 6.5 percent, so interest is 390,000 a year, every year, with a prepayment cost if you repay early. Option two: floating, starting at 5.5 percent, so interest starts at 330,000 but has no ceiling. Option three: floating at 5.5 percent with a cap at 7.5 percent bought for a premium of 150,000 paid at closing, about 50,000 a year spread over three years.

If rates stay flat, option two costs 990,000 over three years, option three costs 1,140,000 including the premium, and option one costs 1,170,000. If rates jump to 9 percent from year two, option two costs 330,000 plus 540,000 plus 540,000, or 1,410,000, while option three is held at 7.5 percent in years two and three: 330,000 plus 450,000 plus 450,000, plus the premium, or 1,380,000, and option one is still 1,170,000. The cap is insurance: it costs you in the good case and protects you in the bad one. Fixed costs most when rates fall and least when they rise. There is no free option, only a choice of which case you are willing to lose in.

How the best do it

Large institutional owners tend to follow a discipline a small developer can copy. They match the rate type and the term of the debt to the business plan: long-hold stabilised assets on long fixed-rate debt, short value-add plans on floating debt with a hedge that runs to the expected exit. They spread loan maturities across different years so that no single bad year forces every refinance at once. And they decide the hedge before they decide the loan amount, so the hedge shapes the size rather than being bolted on afterwards.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's view of your personal balance sheet. The project loan does not appear on your personal statement if the project company is the borrower, but every guarantee you give does, as a contingent liability: a debt that becomes yours if a trigger is hit. Record each one at its full potential amount, not at your estimate of the likelihood. Then compare the total against your liquidity floor, the cash you keep untouched for emergencies. If a single guarantee called in a bad year would breach that floor, the project is carrying more of your personal risk than its return justifies. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any of this.

A third case: the leverage break-even

You can calculate the exact point at which your loan stops helping. Using the first example, the break-even rate is the yield on cost, 7 percent: at that rate interest on 6,000,000 is 420,000 and cash flow to equity is 280,000, which is exactly 7 percent of 4,000,000, the same as owning the building with no debt. Every point above 7 percent costs the equity 60,000 a year, which is 1.5 points of cash-on-cash on a 4,000,000 cheque. Write that break-even on page one of every pro forma. When a lender quotes you a floating rate, you can see immediately how many rate rises stand between you and negative leverage. If the answer is one or two ordinary moves, the leverage is a liability dressed as a benefit.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is borrowing at a cost close to the property's yield, so a small rate rise flips leverage negative. The control is to calculate the yield on cost and the all-in loan cost side by side, and to insist on a spread between them that survives the stressed rate.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner compares only the starting rate of fixed and floating options. Compare the total cost across a flat case and a stressed case, including the hedge premium and any prepayment cost.

Callback

In week 15 we learned that levered IRR can flatter a deal and hide risk. This lesson shows the mechanism: leverage moves the sale gain or loss onto a smaller equity cheque. Always report unlevered IRR beside levered IRR, so the reader can see how much of the return is the asset and how much is the borrowing.

Recap

Debt helps equity only while the property yields more than the loan costs. Levered IRR magnifies gains and losses alike. Fixed, floating and capped debt each lose in a different case, so price all three across a flat and a stressed path. And record every guarantee on your personal balance sheet at its full amount.

Next: LEX on the rules: the covenants, cash controls and hedging terms written into a loan agreement.
checklist: Calculate yield on cost and all-in loan cost side by side
Confirm the spread survives the stressed rate
Report unlevered and levered IRR together
Price fixed, floating and capped debt across a flat and a stressed path
Include hedge premiums and prepayment costs in the comparison
Match the debt term and rate type to the business plan
Record every guarantee at full amount as a contingent liability
Compare total guarantees with your liquidity floor

With 6,000,000 borrowed at 5 percent, equity earns 10 percent cash-on-cash. At 8 percent, equity earns 5.5, worse than owning the building outright. The switch sits where the rate equals the yield on cost. Levered IRR magnifies both ways, because the sale gain or loss lands on the smaller equity cheque. terms: Positive leverage — when the property's yield exceeds the cost of debt, so borrowing raises the return on equity.
Negative leverage — when the cost of debt exceeds the property's yield, so borrowing lowers the return on equity.
Contingent liability — an obligation, such as a guarantee, that becomes payable only if a stated event occurs.

hostile.q: Your yield on cost is 7 percent and your loan costs 6.5. Why is that enough?
hostile.a: On its own it is not; half a point of spread disappears with one rate move. That is why the loan is fixed for the full term, so the cost cannot rise, and why coverage is 1.38 at that fixed rate. If the rate were floating I would borrow less or buy a cap, because the leverage would flip negative at 7 percent.

title: Covenants, cash traps and hedges: what the loan agreement really says
summary: The term sheet sets the size; the loan agreement sets the rules you live under for years. This lesson reads the financial covenants, the cash controls that trap income when a test slips, and the hedging terms, including the cost of unwinding a swap early.
body:
The loan agreement turns the lender's sizing tests into continuing promises. Read it for three things: how each financial covenant is defined and tested, what happens to your cash when a test slips, and what you owe if you break a hedge early.

Recall

Q. What is negative leverage?

A. When the cost of debt exceeds the property's yield, so borrowing lowers the return on equity rather than raising it.

Q. What does a title search tell a lender?

A. Who owns the land and what is registered against it, such as mortgages, easements and encumbrances, so the lender knows what will rank ahead of or alongside its security.

Q. What makes a feasibility study decision-grade?

A. Demand and absorption expressed as numbers, competing supply counted unit by unit, and a go or no-go threshold set before the analysis is run.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the headline terms win you the loan, and the definitions decide whether you keep control of your cash. Two loans with the same coverage covenant can behave entirely differently if one measures NOI before reserves and the other after, or one tests each quarter on the last twelve months and the other on one annualised quarter. What follows is commercial practice in loan documents, not law or a standard, and the terms differ by lender and by country. Professional sign-off required: a lawyer qualified in the loan's governing law, and an independent hedge adviser for any derivative.

Financial covenants: the definitions are the covenant

A financial covenant is a promise in the loan agreement to keep a measured figure above or below a stated level for the life of the loan, such as coverage of at least 1.20 or loan-to-value of no more than 65 percent. The professional reads four parts of every covenant.

First, the definition of income. Does NOI deduct a management fee even if you manage the building yourself? Does it deduct a replacement reserve? Is income from a short-term or non-recurring source excluded? Second, the definition of debt service: interest only, or interest plus scheduled principal, and is it calculated at the actual rate, the capped rate, or a stressed sizing rate? Third, the test period: a trailing twelve months, or the latest quarter multiplied by four? Fourth, the cure: can you put in cash or pay down the loan to restore the ratio, how many times, and within how many days?

Here is the first worked example. A hypothetical building has trailing twelve-month income, before a management fee, of 1,000,000 dollars, and debt service of 800,000. Coverage on that basis is 1.25. If the lender's definition deducts a deemed management fee of 3 percent of revenue, say 45,000 on revenue of 1,500,000, and a replacement reserve of 250 dollars a unit on 100 units, 25,000, the covenant NOI is 930,000 and covenant coverage is about 1.16. Below a 1.20 covenant. Same building, same month, two different answers, and only the one in the definition counts.

Say that out loud now.

Cash controls: the trap before the default

Many loans set two levels on the same ratio. The lower one is the default level, where the lender may accelerate the loan. The higher one is a cash management trigger. When coverage slips below that higher level, a cash sweep begins: rents flow into an account the lender controls, the lender pays itself debt service and approved expenses, and the remaining surplus is held as extra security or applied to pay down the loan instead of being distributed to the owner.

The second worked example. A loan has a default covenant at 1.15 and a cash sweep at 1.30. Coverage falls from 1.40 to 1.28. Nothing is in default, but the owner, who expected distributions of 200,000 dollars that year, receives nothing, because every surplus dollar is trapped until coverage is back above 1.30 for a stated number of consecutive quarters. Investors who were promised a cash yield ask why. The answer is a clause that most people never read because it only matters in a mediocre year, which is exactly the year that comes most often.

Read three things in the cash control clause: the trigger level, the release test (how many quarters above the level before the trap ends), and where trapped cash goes. Cash that is held and later released is very different from cash applied permanently against principal.

Hedges: the second contract

A hedge is a separate contract, usually with a bank, often the lender's own derivatives desk. Swaps and caps between institutions are commonly documented under a standard master agreement published by the International Swaps and Derivatives Association, with a schedule and a confirmation setting the deal terms. The loan agreement then requires the hedge, sets the minimum credit rating of the counterparty, and takes the hedge as part of the lender's security.

The term to understand is breakage cost: what one party owes the other to end a swap early. If you fix a rate with a swap and rates later fall, the swap has a negative value to you, and ending it early, for example to sell or refinance, means paying that value. That payment can be large enough to decide whether the sale is worth doing. A cap carries no breakage cost to you, because you paid the premium at the start; at worst it expires worthless. That asymmetry is often the deciding point when the business plan might end early.

Two more clauses that bite in a mediocre year

Two further clauses deserve a careful read because they work quietly. The first is the reporting covenant: the promise to deliver quarterly statements, an annual budget and the compliance certificate by stated dates. Missing a deadline is often itself an event of default, even when every ratio is healthy, so the reporting calendar belongs in your operating diary with the same weight as the payment dates.

The second is the prepayment clause. Many fixed-rate loans carry a charge for repaying early, calculated to compensate the lender for the interest it loses. Read it alongside any swap. If you fixed the rate with a swap on a floating loan, you may face a breakage cost on the swap and no charge on the loan; if you took a fixed-rate loan, the charge sits inside the loan itself. Either way, ask your lawyer to put an indicative figure on early repayment at two or three dates, so the exit decision later is a calculation rather than a surprise.

Read the notice clause too: how a default notice must be served, to whom, and when any cure period starts running.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is agreeing a covenant number without agreeing its definition, then discovering after closing that the defined NOI is several percent below your own. The control is to rebuild the covenant calculation, line by line, from the draft definitions before signing, using your actual operating statement, and to negotiate the definitions with the same energy as the ratio.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks the default covenant is the one that matters. The cash sweep trigger sits higher and bites first; in most mediocre years it is the only one that ever fires.

Callback

In week 20 we learned that conditions and remedies decide what a contract really does. A covenant is a condition, a cash sweep is a remedy, and the definitions decide when each applies. Read a loan agreement the way you read any contract: what has to be true, and what happens when it is not.

Recap

Every covenant has four parts: the income definition, the debt service definition, the test period and the cure. Cash sweeps trigger above the default level and trap distributions. Hedges are separate contracts; swaps can carry breakage costs and caps cannot. Rebuild each covenant from the definitions before you sign.

Next: Priya with the numbers, in reverse: starting from the loan a lender offered and working back to the income and value it must have assumed.
checklist: Read the income definition used in each covenant
Read the debt service definition and the rate it uses
Note the test period: trailing twelve months or annualised quarter
Note the cure right, its frequency limit and its deadline
Find the cash sweep trigger and its release test
Confirm where trapped cash goes and whether it is released
Ask for an indicative breakage cost before signing any swap
Professional sign-off required: lawyer in the governing law and an independent hedge adviser
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, the loan agreement in one minute. The term sheet sets the size; the loan agreement turns the sizing tests into continuing promises called financial covenants. Every covenant has four parts: how income is defined, how debt service is defined, the test period, and the cure. A building with 1,000,000 of income and 800,000 of debt service covers 1.25 on my numbers, but deduct a deemed management fee and a reserve and covenant coverage is 1.16, below a 1.20 covenant. Above the default level sits a cash sweep trigger: if coverage slips below it, the lender traps every surplus dollar until the ratio recovers. Hedges are separate contracts, often under a standard derivatives master agreement. A swap can carry a breakage cost if I end it early; a cap cannot. So I rebuild every covenant from the draft definitions, using my real statement, before I sign.
terms: Financial covenant — a continuing promise in a loan agreement to keep a measured figure, such as coverage, above or below a stated level.
Cash sweep — a loan mechanism that diverts a property's surplus cash to a lender-controlled account when a ratio falls below a trigger.
Breakage cost — the payment owed to end a hedging contract, such as a swap, before its scheduled end.

hostile.q: You say coverage is 1.25. Which definition are you using?
hostile.a: My own operating statement, before a management fee and reserve, which is not the covenant. On the draft loan definitions, with a deemed 3 percent management fee and the per-unit reserve, covenant coverage is 1.16. So before we sign I want either a covenant at 1.10 on those definitions, or the definitions changed to match how the building is actually run, and a cure right I can exercise twice.

title: Reverse engineering a loan offer: what the lender must have assumed
summary: Start from the loan amount a lender offered and work backward to the income, value and rate it must have used. The gap between the lender's assumptions and yours tells you exactly which number to argue about, and what the project needs to earn for a larger loan.
body:
A loan offer is a finished answer that hides its working. Work backward from the amount and the stated tests, and you can recover the income and value the lender believed, which tells you precisely where its view of your building differs from yours.

Recall

Q. In a loan agreement, what is a cash sweep?

A. A mechanism that diverts surplus cash to a lender-controlled account when a coverage or similar ratio falls below a trigger set above the default level.

Q. What does debt yield ignore that coverage does not?

A. The interest rate. Debt yield is NOI divided by the loan, so it measures the loan's size against income regardless of what the loan costs.

Q. In feasibility, how do you turn competing supply into a number?

A. Count the competing units by delivery date and price band, then reduce your share of demand and slow your absorption for each period they overlap with your lease-up or sales.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, when a lender offers less than you expected, the instinct is to ask for more. That rarely works, because you do not know which assumption produced the number. Reverse engineering turns the offer into a list of the lender's beliefs, and each belief can be supported, challenged or accepted. This is the even-week discipline: start from the outcome and work back to the causes. All numbers are hypothetical.

Step 1: write down the offer and the stated tests

A lender offers a loan of 8,400,000 dollars on a stabilised building. The term sheet states: maximum loan-to-value 60 percent, minimum debt yield 10 percent, minimum coverage 1.30 calculated at a sizing loan constant of 9 percent. A sizing constant is a deliberately conservative rate, higher than the actual rate, that the lender uses only to size the loan, so the loan survives a rise in rates. Your own figures are NOI of 1,000,000 dollars and an appraised value of 16,000,000.

Step 2: run each test backward

Ask, for each test, what input would have produced exactly 8,400,000.

Loan-to-value: 8,400,000 divided by 0.60 is a value of 14,000,000 dollars. If loan-to-value bound, the lender used a value of 14,000,000, not 16,000,000.

Debt yield: 8,400,000 multiplied by 0.10 is NOI of 840,000 dollars. If debt yield bound, the lender underwrote NOI of 840,000.

Coverage: the annual debt service on 8,400,000 at a 9 percent constant is 756,000 dollars. At 1.30 coverage, NOI must be 756,000 multiplied by 1.30, or 982,800 dollars. If coverage bound, the lender underwrote NOI of about 982,800.

Step 3: test which story is consistent

Now run your own numbers forward through the same tests. Loan-to-value at your value of 16,000,000: 9,600,000. Debt yield at your NOI of 1,000,000: 10,000,000. Coverage at your NOI: 1,000,000 divided by 1.30 is 769,231 of debt service, divided by 0.09 is about 8,547,000. On your numbers, coverage would bind at about 8,547,000. The offer is 8,400,000, slightly lower. So the lender did not simply run your figures. Its offer is consistent with a lower NOI: an underwritten NOI of about 982,800 on the coverage test, which is 17,200 dollars below yours.

But check the debt yield story too: if the lender had underwritten 840,000, the coverage test on that NOI would give 840,000 divided by 1.30, divided by 0.09, about 7,180,000, which is below the offer, so that story is inconsistent. The consistent explanation is coverage binding on an NOI of about 983,000.

Say that out loud now.

Step 4: find the difference

A gap of about 17,000 dollars on 1,000,000 is under 2 percent. Lenders typically make adjustments of exactly this size: a deemed management fee where you self-manage, a replacement reserve per unit, or a vacancy allowance above your actual vacancy. Ask the lender for its underwriting adjustments. You will usually find one or two lines, and you now know their total within a few thousand dollars before they tell you.

Step 5: work backward from the loan you want

The second worked example runs the reverse question: what must be true for a loan of 9,000,000? Debt yield: 9,000,000 at 10 percent needs underwritten NOI of 900,000, which you already exceed. Loan-to-value: 9,000,000 divided by 0.60 needs a value of 15,000,000, which your appraisal supports. Coverage: 9,000,000 at 9 percent is 810,000 of debt service, multiplied by 1.30 needs underwritten NOI of 1,053,000. So the only test standing between you and 9,000,000 is coverage at the sizing constant. You need the lender's underwritten NOI to rise from about 983,000 to 1,053,000, an increase of about 70,000 dollars, or the sizing constant to fall, or the coverage minimum to fall.

That converts a vague request for "more loan" into three specific negotiations. Can you show signed leases or a rent roll that supports 70,000 more NOI? Can the lender size at, say, 8.5 percent if you buy a cap that holds the actual rate well below that? Will it accept 1.25 coverage at the sizing rate? Each has a different chance of success, and you can choose the one with the best evidence.

Step 6: check the units

Every figure is in dollars a year except loan amounts and value, which are dollars. Ratios have no units. Percentages applied to a loan give dollars a year; percentages applied to a value give dollars. A reverse engineer who mixes annual and total amounts will get an answer that looks plausible and is wrong by a factor of years.

A second reverse case: the construction loan

The same method works before a building exists. A lender offers a construction loan of 9,750,000 dollars against a hypothetical total cost of 15,000,000, and states a maximum loan-to-cost of 70 percent and a maximum loan-to-value of 60 percent on the as-complete appraisal. Run the tests backward. Loan-to-cost: 9,750,000 divided by 0.70 implies a cost of about 13,930,000, below your 15,000,000, which is inconsistent unless the lender excluded some costs. Loan-to-value: 9,750,000 divided by 0.60 implies an as-complete value of 16,250,000. If your appraisal shows 17,000,000, then loan-to-value did not bind either. So the lender must have removed about 1,070,000 of your costs from the eligible cost base, perhaps a developer fee or a land value above purchase price. Ask which costs are ineligible. The answer tells you how much equity you must bring that does not count towards the lender's test.

Notice what the method gave you in both cases: not a better loan, but a precise question. "Which costs are ineligible?" and "Which income adjustment did you make?" are questions a lender can answer in one email. "Can you do more?" is a question it answers with a polite no.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is arguing the wrong number: pushing for a higher value when coverage binds, or a lower rate when debt yield binds. The control is to identify the binding test from the offer itself before you open the negotiation.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner assumes the lender used his numbers. It almost never does. Assume an adjustment exists, find its size by reverse engineering, then ask the lender to name it.

Callback

In week 17 we reverse engineered a deal from public information: the implied land price, rent and return. This is the same method applied to your own lender. A finished number plus its stated rules lets you recover the hidden assumption, whether the number is a sale price or a loan offer.

Recap

Write down the offer and every stated test. Run each test backward to the input it implies. Keep only the story that is consistent with all tests. Measure the gap from your own numbers, and work backward from the loan you want to find the single input that must change.

Next: Priya in the room: sitting across from a lender's credit officer as the term sheet is negotiated.
checklist: Write the offered amount and every stated sizing test
Run each test backward to the input it implies
Run your own figures forward through the same tests
Keep the story consistent with every test
Measure the gap between the lender's implied income and yours
Ask the lender to name its underwriting adjustments
Work backward from the loan you want to find the one input to change
Check every figure for annual versus total units
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, reverse engineering a loan offer in one minute. A lender offers 8,400,000 with tests of 60 percent loan-to-value, 10 percent debt yield, and 1.30 coverage at a 9 percent sizing constant. Run each test backward. Loan-to-value implies a value of 14,000,000. Debt yield implies income of 840,000. Coverage implies 756,000 of debt service and income of about 983,000. Only the coverage story is consistent with every test, and it sits about 17,000 below my income of 1,000,000, which is the size of a deemed management fee or reserve. Then work backward from the loan I want. For 9,000,000, coverage needs underwritten income of 1,053,000. That is the only test in the way. So I negotiate one thing with evidence: 70,000 more supported income, a lower sizing constant backed by a cap, or a lower coverage minimum.
terms: Sizing constant — a deliberately conservative interest or loan constant a lender uses only to calculate the maximum loan.
Underwritten NOI — the net operating income a lender accepts after its own adjustments, which is usually lower than the borrower's figure.
Reverse engineering — working backward from a finished number and its stated rules to recover the assumptions that produced it.

hostile.q: Why should we raise the loan to 9,000,000 when our underwriting says 8,400,000?
hostile.a: Because only coverage at the sizing constant binds, and I can close most of the gap with evidence. Your offer implies underwritten income of about 983,000. I have signed leases supporting 1,040,000, and I will buy a cap at a strike well below your 9 percent sizing rate. At 8.75 percent sizing and my supported income, coverage at 9,000,000 is about 1.32, above your minimum.

title: In the room with a lender's credit officer
summary: A realistic meeting to negotiate a term sheet with the credit officer who will present the loan to the lender's credit committee. The lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind every question, when to stay silent, and how to hold your state when the offer comes in below plan.
body:
The credit officer is not your opponent; she is the person who has to defend your loan to a committee you will never meet. Give her a case she can defend, and she becomes your advocate in the room you are not in.

Recall

Q. What does reverse engineering a loan offer reveal?

A. The income, value or rate the lender must have assumed, which shows which test binds and which single input must change for a larger loan.

Q. What is the purpose of a mock go or no-go meeting before a land purchase?

A. To rehearse the decision against stated thresholds, under hostile questions, so the real decision rests on evidence rather than momentum.

Q. What does a cash sweep do?

A. It traps surplus cash in a lender-controlled account when a ratio falls below a trigger, before any default.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, most of a loan's terms are fixed in a single meeting and the follow-up calls after it. The documents that follow mostly record what was agreed in that room. A developer who arrives with a story gets a loan sized to the lender's caution. A developer who arrives with the lender's own tests already run gets a conversation about evidence.

The scene

This is a composite example. You are refinancing a hypothetical stabilised building with NOI of 1,000,000 dollars. You want 9,000,000. The term sheet in front of you offers 8,400,000, with coverage of 1.30 at a 9 percent sizing constant, a cash sweep at 1.35, and a springing guarantee on coverage below 1.15. The credit officer, Ms Daley, opens: "We like the asset. We are where we are on proceeds."

The lines to say

Open with the bottom line: "I want to close at 9,000,000, and I think only one of your four tests is in the way." Then show the table: loan-to-value, debt yield and coverage at both her numbers and yours, binding test marked. This tells her you have done her work, and it narrows the conversation to one number.

Then ask the precise question: "Your offer implies underwritten income of about 983,000. Is the adjustment the management fee, the reserve, or vacancy?" She will usually tell you. Suppose she says a deemed management fee of 3 percent. You reply with evidence, not argument: "Here is a third-party management agreement at that fee, already in my operating statement. Your adjustment double counts it." That is a sentence she can repeat to her committee.

On the guarantee: "I will accept a guarantee for fraud, misconduct and environmental losses. I will not guarantee a coverage ratio, because that asks me to fund losses in exactly the year the building is weakest. In exchange I will fund a cap to term and a debt service reserve." You have offered her protection in a form her committee prefers to a personal promise from one person.

Say that out loud now.

The lines never to say

Never say "the other bank will do 9.5." Unless it is true and in writing, it costs you credibility the moment she asks for the term sheet. Never say "rates will come down by then." She has heard it in every cycle and her committee has a slide about it. Never say "the guarantee is fine, it will never be called." If it will never be called, you lose nothing by asking for it to be removed, and you have just told her you have not read it.

The question behind the question

When she asks, "What is your plan if rates stay high?", she is not asking about rates. She is asking whether you will still be solvent and still in charge in year three. Answer that question: "At the sizing constant, coverage is 1.32 on my supported income; the cap holds the actual rate below the sizing rate; and I have a twelve-month debt service reserve. I do not need rates to fall to stay current." When she asks, "Who else is in the deal?", she is asking who absorbs a loss before her bank does. Answer with the equity and its terms.

When to stay silent

After you state the number you want and the evidence for it, stop. A silence of five seconds feels long to you and normal to her. If you fill it, you will usually fill it with a concession. Silence is also right when she says something you disagree with that does not matter to the outcome: let it go, and spend your credibility on the one test that binds.

How to hold your state

The offer arriving below plan produces a quick spike of frustration, and frustration speaks faster and louder than it should. Before the meeting, decide your walk-away number in writing, here perhaps 8,700,000 with no coverage guarantee. Then nothing in the room can surprise you into a worse deal. A slow exhale before you answer a hard point gives you two seconds and lowers your voice, a practitioner habit rather than a research finding. Speak at the pace you would use to brief a control room: steady, short sentences, numbers stated once and clearly.

How the outcome is measured

The second worked example is the result. Ms Daley removes the double-counted management fee, raising underwritten income to about 1,013,000. She agrees to size at 8.75 percent because of the cap. Coverage at 9,000,000 is 9,000,000 multiplied by 0.0875, which is 787,500 of debt service; 1,013,000 divided by 787,500 is about 1.29. Just short of 1.30. You agree to 8,900,000: debt service of 778,750 and coverage of about 1.30. And the guarantee becomes fraud and environmental only. You moved 500,000 dollars of proceeds and removed a personal exposure, without raising your voice.

Working with advisers

This month's thread is advisers. The bank that lends to you will often also offer to sell you the cap or swap. That is not wrong, but the bank is then on both sides of a price you cannot easily check. An independent hedge adviser, paid by you and not by any bank, can tell you whether the premium or the swap rate is fair and what breakage might cost later.

Instruct every adviser in writing: what decision their advice supports, what they must check, and the deadline. Ask each one the same closing question: "What would make you change this advice?" The answer tells you what to monitor after closing.

Reading the room as the meeting moves

Watch for three signals during the meeting. When the credit officer starts writing down your evidence rather than listening politely, she has decided to take it to committee; slow down and make sure every figure she records is right. When she says "I will need to check with credit," she is telling you the decision is not hers, so ask what the committee will want to see and offer to provide it in writing by a date. When she moves the conversation to fees, legal costs or timing, the substance is nearly settled. Do not reopen it. Confirm what has been agreed, aloud, before the meeting ends: "So we have 8,900,000, sizing at 8.75 percent, the guarantee limited to fraud and environmental, and I will send the management agreement and the cap quote by Friday." Then send a short email the same day recording it. A term sheet drafted from your summary is easier to correct than one drafted from her memory.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk in the room is negotiating the rate while the guarantee and the cash sweep pass unremarked. The control is to list the five terms that decide your downside before the meeting, and to refuse to close the meeting until each has been discussed.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats the credit officer as a gatekeeper to be persuaded. She is an advocate who needs ammunition. Give her evidence she can repeat.

Callback

In week 6 we practised hostile questions: acknowledge, bridge, answer, and commit to confirm by a date. Every hard question in this meeting follows that pattern: acknowledge the lender's concern, bridge to the binding test, answer with the number, and promise the document by Friday.

Recap

Arrive with the lender's tests already run. Ask which adjustment produced the gap, answer with evidence, trade personal guarantees for structural protection, stay silent after your number, and decide your walk-away figure before you enter.

Next: Kema, with Cole in the Auditor's Chair, closes the week on debt with six questions and a hostile read of a compliance certificate.
checklist: Prepare the four-test table at the lender's numbers and yours
Write your walk-away amount and terms before the meeting
Ask which underwriting adjustment produced the gap
Bring third-party evidence for every disputed income line
Offer structural protection in place of a coverage guarantee
List the five downside terms and discuss each before leaving
Stay silent after stating your number
Engage an independent hedge adviser for any cap or swap
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, the credit meeting in one minute. The credit officer must defend my loan to a committee I will never meet, so I give her a case she can repeat. I open with the number and the one test in the way. I show all four tests at her numbers and mine. I ask which adjustment produced the gap and answer it with a document. I refuse to guarantee a coverage ratio and offer a cap to term and a reserve instead. I never quote a rival bank I cannot show, never promise rates will fall, and never call a guarantee a formality. After stating my number I stay silent. I decide my walk-away before the meeting. In this case, removing a double-counted fee and sizing at 8.75 percent moved the loan from 8,400,000 to 8,900,000 and limited the guarantee to fraud and environmental loss.
terms: Credit officer — the lender's employee who analyses a loan and presents it to the credit committee for approval.
Walk-away number — the least acceptable outcome, decided in writing before a negotiation begins.
Debt service reserve — cash held for the lender's benefit, sized to cover a stated number of months of loan payments.

hostile.q: Why should we take the guarantee off the coverage covenant? It is our protection.
hostile.a: Because it protects you in the year I am least able to pay, which makes it weak protection. I am offering stronger protection that does not depend on my personal position: a cap to the full term, a twelve-month debt service reserve funded at closing, and a cash sweep at 1.35. Those protect you whatever happens to me.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 36 review: debt, from sizing to hedges
summary: Six questions on loan sizing, coverage, debt yield, leverage and hedges, a recap of the week, Cole's Auditor's Chair on a hypothetical quarterly compliance certificate, and a two-minute boardroom explanation with a model answer.
body:
This week came down to one idea: a loan is sized by its tightest test, lives under its definitions, and survives only if it still works at the rate you did not expect. You should now be able to size, stress and read any loan offer in one sitting.

Recall

Q. What is a sizing constant?

A. A deliberately conservative rate a lender uses only to calculate the maximum loan, so the loan still covers if real rates rise.

Q. What does a directors' resolution authorising a loan need to show?

A. That the company approved the borrowing and named who may sign, recorded properly in the minute book.

Q. Why count competing supply unit by unit?

A. Because each competing unit delivered during your lease-up takes a share of the same demand and slows your absorption in that period.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a review turns a week of lessons into a habit you can use under pressure. Answer each question aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. What is the binding limit? Answer: The smallest loan amount produced by the lender's tests, coverage, debt yield, loan-to-value and loan-to-cost. That test decides the size, and it tells you which input to work on.

Question 2. Why does debt yield matter when rates are low? Answer: Because it ignores the interest rate. A low rate can make coverage look comfortable, but debt yield still caps the loan to what the income would earn the lender if it owned the building.

Question 3. When does leverage lower the return on equity? Answer: When the all-in cost of the debt exceeds the property's yield on cost. Then each borrowed dollar loses money and equity pays the difference.

Question 4. Why can a cap be safer than a swap if the plan may end early? Answer: A cap's cost is a premium paid up front, so ending early costs nothing more. A swap can carry a breakage cost if rates have moved against you.

Question 5. In the reverse-engineering lesson, which test explained the 8,400,000 offer? Answer: Coverage at the 9 percent sizing constant, on underwritten income of about 983,000, about 17,000 below the borrower's figure.

Question 6. What is Rule 36? Answer: I never sign floating-rate debt unless the project still meets its coverage covenant at the hedged or stressed rate for the full term, and I never sign a guarantee whose trigger is a test I have not stressed at that rate.

Say that out loud now.

Week recap

Day 1 ran the four sizing tests and found the binding limit. Day 2 took apart a composite in which a performing building was lost to a floating loan, a short cap and a springing guarantee. Day 3 showed positive and negative leverage and priced fixed, floating and capped debt. Day 4 read covenants, cash sweeps and hedging terms. Day 5 worked backward from an offer to the lender's assumptions. Day 6 negotiated the evidence, not the mood.

Auditor's Chair

This week the Red Pen becomes Cole's Auditor's Chair. Read this hypothetical quarterly compliance certificate as a hostile auditor would: assume each figure is flattering until proved otherwise.

Compliance certificate, quarter ended 30 June. Net operating income for the quarter, 300,000 dollars, annualised to 1,200,000. Debt service for the year, interest only at the capped rate of 6 percent on 15,000,000, 900,000. Coverage 1.33, above the 1.20 covenant and the 1.30 cash management trigger; no sweep required. Management fee not deducted, as the borrower self-manages. Replacement reserve deferred this quarter. The cap expires on 31 August and a replacement is being sourced. Signed by the borrower's managing director.

Cole's findings. First, annualising one quarter: if the second quarter is seasonally strong, multiplying it by four overstates the year. The auditor asks for the trailing twelve months and the covenant's actual test period. Second, debt service at the capped rate: if the loan definition uses the actual rate, or the cap expires within the test period, the figure is wrong. Third, the management fee: most loan definitions deduct a deemed fee even when the owner self-manages; at 3 percent of a hypothetical 1,800,000 of revenue that is 54,000, which takes annualised NOI to 1,146,000 and coverage to about 1.27, below the 1.30 trigger. Fourth, a deferred reserve inflates NOI if the definition requires the reserve deduction. Fifth, the cap expiry two months away is a known event inside the next test period and should be disclosed with its replacement cost and the coverage at the uncapped rate. Sixth, the certificate is signed by the borrower alone, with no supporting schedule. The auditor's verdict: a sweep is probably already required, and the certificate as written would mislead the lender.

Boardroom drill

Explain this week's debt to a board in two minutes. Try it now, aloud, then compare with this model answer.

Model answer: "We are borrowing 8,900,000 against a building earning about 1,000,000 a year. The lender sized the loan on coverage at a conservative 8.75 percent rate, which is the test that binds; debt yield and loan-to-value would allow more. The rate is floating, and we have bought a cap to the full five-year term that holds the actual rate below the sizing rate, so coverage stays at about 1.30 or better in the worst rate case. Distributions stop if coverage falls below 1.35, which our downside case does not reach. The only personal guarantee covers fraud and environmental loss, not performance. The main risk is a fall in income, not in rates, and a 10 percent income fall still keeps us above the default covenant."

Score yourself

Record your two-minute answer on your phone and score it 1 to 5 on four things. Accuracy: were the tests and the binding limit right? Structure: did you open with the amount and the binding test? Composure: was your pace steady, with a pause after each key number? The hard question: did you say what happens if rates rise and the cap expires?

Where you will meet this again

Debt sizing runs through the rest of this phase. In week 37 the capital stack sits on top of the senior loan you sized this week, and every junior layer is tested by cumulative coverage, the same ratio extended upward. In weeks 39 and 40 the construction lender applies loan-to-cost during the build and converts your covenants into conditions on each draw. In week 44 the stress tests will be run against exactly the coverage and break-even rate you learned here. Keep your four-test table and your leverage break-even on one page, and reuse them every time a lender sends a term sheet.

One practical habit before next week: take any loan offer you can find, real or hypothetical, and spend fifteen minutes running it through the four tests and the reverse-engineering steps. Speed comes only from repetition.

A second habit: when any lender quotes you a floating rate, say the leverage break-even aloud before you say anything else. It keeps the rate in its proper place, as one input among several.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is a loan that works only at today's rate and today's definitions. The control is coverage at the stressed rate, on the lender's definitions, for the full term.

The beginner's mistake

Reading the amount and the rate and nothing else. The tests, definitions, sweeps and guarantees are the loan.

Callback

In week 11 we learned that profit and cash are different things. This week showed it again: a building can be profitable while a cash sweep stops every dollar reaching you, and a coverage breach can occur while the property still earns a healthy accounting profit.

Recap

Size to the tightest test, stress coverage at the rate you fear, read every definition, hedge to the term, and keep your personal guarantees limited to conduct you control.

speak: Mr Shabazz, week 36 in sixty seconds. A lender runs coverage, debt yield, loan-to-value and loan-to-cost and lends the smallest answer, the binding limit. Debt yield ignores the rate, so it caps a loan even when money is cheap. Leverage helps equity only while the property yields more than the debt costs. Fixed, floating and capped debt each lose in a different case; a cap's cost is paid up front, while a swap can carry breakage. The loan agreement turns sizing tests into covenants, and the definitions decide the answer, with a cash sweep sitting above the default level. Reverse engineering an offer recovers the lender's assumptions. In the room, bring the tests already run and trade guarantees for structure. The composite case gave Rule 36: floating debt must still meet its covenant at the hedged or stressed rate for the full term, and no guarantee on a test I have not stressed.
terms: Binding limit — the smallest loan produced by a lender's sizing tests, which therefore sets the amount.
Compliance certificate — a periodic statement by a borrower to a lender showing the calculation of each financial covenant.
Test period — the span of time over which a financial covenant is measured, such as a trailing twelve months.
